intro: An experiment is only fair if chance decides who gets which treatment. Randomize, run the experiment, and see where the estimated effect lands. Run it a hundred times and the dots show what each design buys you: random assignment centers the estimate on the true effect, blocking and pairing make it vary less, and letting someone choose builds in confounding.
howItWorks:
Each unit has its own baseline response, fixed once from a seed: sunny pots grow taller and older volunteers recall fewer words, whatever the treatment. A run adds the true treatment effect to every unit that gets treatment A, plus a little measurement noise, so the estimate (mean of A minus mean of B) can be compared with the effect that was built in.

  • Completely randomized. Half of all the units, chosen at random, get treatment A.
  • Blocked. The units are split by the other variable first (sun or shade, younger or older), and half of each block gets A.
  • Matched pairs. Neighbors in the same block form pairs; a coin flip in each pair decides which one gets A.
  • Not random. The gardener or the volunteers choose, and the choice follows the other variable, so its effect mixes with the treatment's.
  • Blinding. In the memory study, volunteers who know they took caffeine expect to do better, and that adds to their scores; a placebo and double blinding remove it.

Test yourself makes new problems from a seed (the problem code), and every key is checked by the validator.

scenes.name: Fertilizer on tomato seedlings

none.note: The gardener gives the new fertilizer to the plants that look healthiest, the ones by the window.

scenes.blockWhy: Pots by the window grow taller whatever they are fed, so each block compares the two fertilizers in the same light.
scenes.pairWhy: Two neighboring pots get the same light, so each pair compares the fertilizers on nearly identical plants.
scenes.noneWhy: The sunny pots got the new fertilizer and grow taller anyway, so sunlight is confounded with fertilizer: the estimate is too big.

scenes.name: Caffeine and memory

none.note: The volunteers choose their own pill, and the younger coffee drinkers mostly choose caffeine.

scenes.blockWhy: Older volunteers recall fewer words whatever pill they take, so each block compares the pills within one age group.
scenes.pairWhy: Two neighbors in the same age group recall about the same, so each pair compares the pills on similar people.
scenes.noneWhy: Younger volunteers chose caffeine, and younger people recall more words anyway, so age is confounded with the pill.
scenes.blindWhy: When volunteers know they took caffeine they expect to remember more, and that expectation alone raises their scores. A placebo that looks the same, with nobody knowing who took which, removes it.

contexts.lead: A garden center tests a new fertilizer on tomato plants.
contexts.measure: measure each plant's height after four weeks
contexts.blockWhy: sunny plants grow taller whatever the fertilizer, so each fertilizer is compared on sunny plants and on shady plants.
contexts.pairsHow: plants of the same starting height
contexts.lurk: how healthy the plants were at the start
contexts.population: tomato plants of this variety in the greenhouse
contexts.obs: The gardener uses the new fertilizer on the plants she thinks look healthiest and the current fertilizer on the rest.
contexts.obsWhy: the healthiest looking plants got the new fertilizer, and healthier plants grow taller anyway.
contexts.sampleRandom: The garden center randomly selects 40 plants from all the tomato plants of this variety in its greenhouse.
contexts.sampleVol: The garden center uses the 40 plants left over on its sale table.
contexts.selfSelect: The workers decide which fertilizer each plant gets.

contexts.lead: Psychologists test whether caffeine improves short-term memory.
contexts.measure: count how many words from a list of 30 each volunteer recalls
contexts.blockWhy: memory changes with age, so each pill is compared among younger and among older volunteers.
contexts.pairsHow: volunteers of the same age and sex
contexts.obs: The volunteers choose their own pill, and most of the younger volunteers choose caffeine.
contexts.obsWhy: younger volunteers chose caffeine more often, and younger people tend to recall more words anyway.
contexts.sampleRandom: The psychologists randomly select 60 adults from the city's list of registered voters, and all agree to take part.
contexts.sampleVol: The psychologists recruit 60 adults who answer a newspaper ad.
contexts.selfSelect: Each volunteer chooses which pill to take.

blind.text: The two pills look identical, and the people scoring the test do not know who took which.
blind.why: neither the volunteers nor the scorers know who took caffeine, so expectations cannot push the results

contexts.lead: A school tests whether an online tutoring program raises math scores.
blocks: students with an A or B
students with a C or lower
contexts.blockWhy: students who already did well tend to score higher, so each kind of support is compared within each grade group.
contexts.pairsHow: students with the same previous math grade
contexts.obs: Students sign up for the tutoring program if they want it; the rest do regular homework.
contexts.obsWhy: students who sign up for extra tutoring are likely more motivated, and motivated students tend to score higher anyway.
contexts.sampleRandom: The school randomly selects 80 students from its list of all students.
contexts.sampleVol: The school asks for volunteers, and 80 students sign up.
contexts.selfSelect: Each student chooses tutoring or regular homework.

blind.text: The teachers who grade the final exam do not know which students had tutoring, but the students know.
blind.who: the graders do not know, the students do
blind.why: the graders cannot score one group more kindly, even without meaning to

contexts.lead: A shoe company compares two sole materials for running shoes.
contexts.measure: measure how much each sole wears down after a month
contexts.selfPairs: Each of the 20 runners wears a shoe with material A on one foot and material B on the other. A coin flip decides which foot gets material A. After a month the company measures how much each sole wore down.
contexts.assignText: A coin flip decides which foot of each runner wears material A; the other foot wears material B.
contexts.result: Material A soles wore down clearly less than material B soles.
contexts.blockWhy: runners who run farther wear out both soles faster.
contexts.pairsHow: the two feet of one runner
contexts.obs: The company compares runners who bought shoes with material A in its stores with runners who bought material B.
contexts.obsWhy: runners who choose one shoe may run farther than those who choose the other, and distance changes sole wear.
contexts.sampleRandom: The company randomly selects 20 runners from its list of running club members.
contexts.sampleVol: The company recruits 20 runners who answer an ad.
contexts.selfSelect: Each runner chooses one material and wears it on both feet.
